--- title: "Environment, Packages, Functions, Import/Export" author: "Enrico Toffalini" include-in-header: ../assets/slidesheader.html format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false css: custom.css theme: default slide-number: c/t self-contained: true code-fold: false code-summary: "Show code" code-overflow: wrap title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: "figures/psicostatLogo.png" data-background-size: "contain" data-background-opacity: "0.15" execute: echo: true output: true --- ## Install packages... and more Most of the data analysis tasks you will perform won’t come from base R: you will most often load additional **packages** for specialized functions ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="39%"} Install a package from CRAN ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("effsize") ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="61%"} Simultaneously install multiple packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages( c("effsize","psych","ggplot2") ) ``` ::: ::: ::: For development or personal use, you may occasionally install packages from outside CRAN, such as from GitHub: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} devtools::install_github("FilippoGambarota/filor") devtools::install_github("EnricoToffalini/toffee") ``` ::: After installing, you need to attach the packages using the `library()` function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(effsize) library(ggplot2) ``` ::: ## Install packages... and more ### call functions After attaching a package, its functions are directly callable throughout the R session: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(psych) fisherz(rho=0.5) # use a function from the "psych" package ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5493061 ``` ::: ::: You may directly call any function from any installed package, even without attaching it, using "**`::`**"; this is especially useful when there is a risk of functions with conflicting names, or if you just don't want to attach an entire package to use a single function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} psych::fisherz(rho=0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5493061 ``` ::: ::: ## #### Some R packages that you will or may need in the future (1/3) | Package | Used for what | Examples of functions |-----|-------------|-----------| | `base`
(base R) | Basic functions | `sum`, `mean`, `sqrt`, `abs`, `c`, `data.frame`, `summary`, `scale`, `plot`, `+`, `-`, `!`, `>` | `stats`
(base R) | Basic statistical calculations and functions | `sd`, `cor`, `cor.test`, `t.test`, `lm`, `glm`, `AIC`, `rnorm`, `rbinom` | `graphics`
(base R) | Basic plotting functions | `plot`, `boxplot`, `hist`, `barplot` :::{.callout-tip} You may actually use the base R packages very often without even realizing that they are packages.
To inspect all currently attached packages, run `search()` ::: ## #### Some R packages that you will or may need in the future (2/3) | Package | Used for what | Examples of functions |-----|--------------|----------| | `lme4` | Fitting (generalized) (non-)linear mixed-effects models | `lmer`, `glmer`, `ranef` | `performance` | Useful tools for models checks and diagnostics | `check_collinearity`, `r2_nagelkerke`, `icc` | `effects` | Display effects for various statistical models | `allEffects`, `effect` | `emmeans` | Estimate marginal means for various models | `emmeans` | `effectsize` | Compute or convert different effect sizes | `cohens_d`, `hedges_g`, `cohens_f`, `d_to_r` ## #### Some R packages that you will or may need in the future (3/3) | Package | Used for what | Examples of functions |-----|--------------|----------| | `ggplot2` | Create beautiful plots using The Grammar of Graphics | `ggplot`, `geom_point`, `geom_line`, ... | `lavaan` | Structural Equation Models (SEM) | `sem`, `cfa` | `semTools` | Useful tools for SEMs | `compRelSEM`, `measEq.syntax` | `metafor` | Meta-analysis | `rma`, `rma.mv`, `forest`, `funnel`, `regtest` | `brms` | Fitting practically any Bayesian model via MCMC with Stan | `brm`, `set_prior` | `blavaan` | Fitting Bayesian SEMs | `bcfa`, `bsem` ## Reproducibility tip: `sessionInfo()` When sharing your full R project, also share info on your **R version, OS, and loaded package versions** for reproducibility ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sessionInfo() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R version 4.5.1 (2025-06-13 ucrt) Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 Running under: Windows 11 x64 (build 22631) Matrix products: default LAPACK version 3.12.1 locale: [1] LC_COLLATE=English_United Kingdom.utf8 [2] LC_CTYPE=English_United Kingdom.utf8 [3] LC_MONETARY=English_United Kingdom.utf8 [4] LC_NUMERIC=C [5] LC_TIME=English_United Kingdom.utf8 time zone: Europe/Rome tzcode source: internal attached base packages: [1] stats graphics grDevices utils datasets methods base other attached packages: [1] ggplot2_4.0.3 semTools_0.5-6 lme4_1.1-36 Matrix_1.6-2 lavaan_0.6-19 [6] psych_2.5.6 loaded via a namespace (and not attached): [1] generics_0.1.3 sandwich_3.1-1 lattice_0.22-6 magrittr_2.0.5 [5] digest_0.6.37 evaluate_1.0.3 grid_4.5.1 estimability_1.5.1 [9] RColorBrewer_1.1-3 mvtnorm_1.3-3 fastmap_1.2.0 jsonlite_2.0.0 [13] survival_3.8-3 multcomp_1.4-28 scales_1.4.0 TH.data_1.1-3 [17] pbivnorm_0.6.0 codetools_0.2-20 mnormt_2.1.1 reformulas_0.4.0 [21] Rdpack_2.6.2 cli_3.6.5 rlang_1.1.7 rbibutils_2.3 [25] splines_4.5.1 withr_3.0.2 yaml_2.3.12 tools_4.5.1 [29] parallel_4.5.1 nloptr_2.1.1 coda_0.19-4.1 minqa_1.2.8 [33] dplyr_1.2.1 boot_1.3-31 vctrs_0.7.1 R6_2.6.1 [37] stats4_4.5.1 zoo_1.8-13 lifecycle_1.0.5 emmeans_1.10.7 [41] MASS_7.3-60 pkgconfig_2.0.3 pillar_1.10.2 gtable_0.3.6 [45] glue_1.8.1 Rcpp_1.0.14 tidyselect_1.2.1 tibble_3.3.0 [49] xfun_0.51 rstudioapi_0.19.0 knitr_1.50 dichromat_2.0-1 [53] farver_2.1.2 xtable_1.8-4 htmltools_0.5.8.1 nlme_3.1-167 [57] rmarkdown_2.30 compiler_4.5.1 quadprog_1.5-8 S7_0.2.0 ``` ::: :::

*Optional:* **`renv::snapshot()`** records package versions so your project environment can be restored later

## Functions and arguments Functions typically take some *input* parameters, known as *arguments*, process them, and yield some *output*/result(s)
## Functions and arguments ### arguments - values or variables you pass to a function as input, or to control its behavior for example, `seq()` generates a sequence of numbers; "`from`" and "`to`" are arguments: it will provide the integers between these two extremes: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} seq(from = 3, to = 7) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 4 5 6 7 ``` ::: ::: `length.out` controls how many equally spaced numbers must be generated: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} seq(from = 3, to = 7, length.out = 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.000000 4.333333 5.666667 7.000000 ``` ::: ::: alternatively, `by` defines the step size between numbers: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} seq(from = 3, to = 7, by = 0.6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.0 3.6 4.2 4.8 5.4 6.0 6.6 ``` ::: ::: ## Functions and arguments ### arguments - values or variables you pass to a function as input, or to control its behavior `rnorm()` will generate "`n`" random numbers from a normal distribution with "`mean`" as the average and "`sd`" as the standard deviation: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rnorm(n = 5, mean = 100, sd = 15) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 75.38222 85.76437 94.26437 105.08416 82.28577 ``` ::: ::: **Positional matching** - argument names may be omitted if placed in the correct order ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rnorm(5, 100, 15) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 96.88712 90.62131 104.77531 98.78010 91.92415 ``` ::: ::: ## Functions and arguments **Default arguments** - a function *might* still work even if some arguments are omitted, if it can use its own *default values* (in this case "`mean=0, sd=1`") ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rnorm(n = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.54426680 0.87785128 -0.09772879 1.97352174 0.44375369 ``` ::: ::: **Errors** - however, omitting mandatory arguments will result in an *Error* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rnorm(mean = 100, sd = 15) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in rnorm(mean = 100, sd = 15): argument "n" is missing, with no default ``` ::: ::: **Warnings** - some inputs may cause the function to produce *Warnings* and bad output, but they do **not** stop code execution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rnorm(n = 5, mean = 100, sd = -15) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning in rnorm(n = 5, mean = 100, sd = -15): NAs produced ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN ``` ::: ::: ## Functions and arguments ### Reproducible randomness: `set.seed()`
Random draws normally change from one call to the next: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rnorm(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5578005 1.7443403 1.9692890 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} rnorm(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.7956037 -0.2073927 0.6115656 ``` ::: :::
Setting the **seed** reproduces the same sequence: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(20261117) rnorm(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.01725691 0.11903041 -1.01027208 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(20261117) rnorm(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.01725691 0.11903041 -1.01027208 ``` ::: :::
:::{.callout-tip} Set the seed once **before a simulation script** if you aim to ensure exact reproducibility (it may not be enough with parallelized computing). ::: ## Functions and arguments ### *HELP!* see the documentation of a function There are two ways to access documentation: using "`?`" and using `help()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ?rnorm # this will work help(rnorm) # this does the same ``` :::
## Some common errors | Error message | What to check | |---|---| | `there is no package called 'psych'` | Install the package first | | `could not find function "fisherz"` | Load `library(psych)` | | `object 'x' not found` | name, or a line not run yet | | `unexpected symbol` / `unexpected ')'` | Commas, parentheses, quotes | | `cannot open file` | File name or path | | `non-numeric argument to binary operator` | number stored as text? | Read the message and locate the **first failing line**. RStudio generally stops execution at first error. ## Set up Working Directory
The **Working Directory** (WD) is the location of the folder on your computer where R reads and saves files by default. Let's see my own WD using the `getwd()` function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} getwd() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "C:/Users/enric/Desktop/Basics-R/Slides" ``` ::: ::: If you import/export anything (*data*, *figures*, *workspaces*, etc.) you need to know your WD!
## Set up Working Directory As a general rule: - When you open R or the RStudio app, the default WD may your `documents` folder (in Windows) or your `home directory` (e.g., `/home/username`; in Linux or macOS); - This default may be changed at any time from inside RStudio via `Tools > Global Options... > General`; - If you open a file (e.g., a `.R` script) using RStudio, the WD is set to that file's location (unless the RStudio app was already open before); - However, you can set a new WD at any time from within the R code, using the **`setwd()`** function, for example: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} setwd("C:/Users/enric/") ``` ::: ## Set up Working Directory ⚠️ **Windows users**, be careful! When you copy-and-paste a folder address, Windows will probably take "`\`" as path separator, but "`\`" is the escape character in R, so you will get an error: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} setwd("C:\Users\enric\") ``` ::: 
Error: '\U' used without hex digits in character string (<input>:1:11)
\ ### How to fix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} setwd("C:\\Users\\enric\\") ``` ::: or ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} setwd( "C:/Users/enric/" ) ``` ::: ## Absolute vs Relative paths - **ABSOLUTE paths**: indicate the full path **from the root**, e.g., `"C:/Users/enric/"` (in Linux it might be `"/home/enric/"`; in macOS `"/Users/enric/"`) - **RELATIVE paths**: indicate the path starting from *(relative to)* the current directory. Most often, you prefer this for import/export, so the same script works on any device; e.g., `"figures/"` or `../figures/` - `png(filename = "figures/Fig1.png")` saves a file `Fig1.png` into `figures`, which is a subfolder **inside** the current WD; - `png(filename = "../figures/Fig1.png")` saves a file `Fig1.png` into `figures`, which is a folder **outside, one level up** (`"../"`) from the current WD ## RStudio Projects
**`.Rproj`** may eliminate the need to use `setwd()` within scripts, so you can use only relative paths
- You can create a *new project* in RStudio with `File > New Project...`, choosing a specific folder - Keep all materials of your project in the same folder as the newly created `.Rproj` file - As you open the `.Rproj`, it will automatically start a new *RStudio* session with the WD set to that folder.
## RStudio Projects Opening the `.Rproj` file ensures that RStudio automatically sets the project folder as the working directory, so all files are managed relative to it:
## Import/export
Now let's see how to perform **import/export** operations for: - **The Workspace**: all objects that exist in your current R session, all results and computations stored so far (see them in the *"Environment" panel* or with `ls()`); - **Data: SUPER IMPORTANT!** we will focus especially on tabular (Excel-like) data, which we treat as dataframes; - **Figures**: save your plots for reports and more in `.pdf`, `.png`, and other formats.
## Import/export ### Workspace All your R code (script) is generally stored in text files with a `.R` extension. But where do you save your results and objects?! Maybe you just don't... However, you can export the entire **workspace** using **`save.image()`** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # let's populate the workspace first N = 100 x = rnorm(N,0,1) y = 2 + 0.6*x + rnorm(N,0,0.8) df = data.frame(x, y) fit = lm(y ~ x, data=df) # now let's save it save.image("myWS.RData") ``` :::

*Specifying `"myWS.RData"` is not mandatory but recommended, otherwise your file will simply be named `".RData"`. (By the way... where will it be saved?)*

## Import/export ### Workspace Alternatively, you can save just one or a few workspace objects using **`save()`** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # let's populate the workspace first N = 100 x = rnorm(N,0,1) y = 2 + 0.6*x + rnorm(N,0,0.8) df = data.frame(x, y) fit = lm(y ~ x, data=df) # now let's save only two objects save(df, fit, file="myWS.RData") ``` ::: This will save only objects `df` and `fit` into a newly created file named `myWS.RData`. This is useful when you have an overcrowded workspace and want to save only a few objects containing the final results ## Import/export ### Workspace Once you open a new R session, you may load the previously stored workspace using the `load()` function, specifying `load("workspace_name.RData")`, like this: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # empty the workspace to make sure there's actually nothing! rm(list=ls()) # now load the previously saved workspace load("myWS.RData") # make sure that the objects have been loaded ls() ``` ::: ## Import/export ### Data
Arguably a **fundamental skill** for anyone working in data science! Most people use *MS Excel* or similar software (e.g., *LibreOffice Calc*) for handling data, which produce their own file formats (e.g., `.xlsx`). That's perfectly fine. However... the **most versatile data format is `.csv` (comma-separated values)**, a simple text (no formatting, no licences required) file format for storing tabular data/dataframes. - **Best practice**: Save data in `.csv` format from your software of choice before importing it into R.
## Import/export ### Data Here's an example of using **`read.csv()`** for **importing** data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # IMPORT csv data from a "data" subfolder, and store it in an object named "df" df = read.csv("data/Performance.csv") # OR if you want to be explicit about settings: df = read.csv("data/Performance.csv", header=TRUE, sep=",", dec=".") head(df) # have a look at the first few rows ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` id name anx acc time 1 1 nydga 20 15 2.077932 2 2 bwknr 14 9 2.436858 3 3 sauuj 18 12 2.549814 4 4 vnjgi 27 15 4.386718 5 5 oueiy 21 11 5.248933 6 6 neebj 12 13 3.463094 ``` ::: :::
⚠️ in Italian Excel export settings, the *separator character* (`sep`) may be "`;`" and the *decimal point character* (`dec`) "`,`", so be aware of your settings!
## Import/export ### Data If you absolutely want to import your data directly from a **MS Excel** document (`.xlsx`), you may use the function **`read_excel()`** from the package `readxl`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(readxl) df = data.frame( read_excel("data/Performance.xlsx") ) # data.frame() forces it to be a dataframe, otherwise it's a tibble head(df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` id name anx acc time 1 1 nydga 20 15 2.077932 2 2 bwknr 14 9 2.436858 3 3 sauuj 18 12 2.549814 4 4 vnjgi 27 15 4.386718 5 5 oueiy 21 11 5.248933 6 6 neebj 12 13 3.463094 ``` ::: :::
- You may even import data from an **SPSS** document (`.sav`) using the `read.spss()` function from the `foreign` package
## Import/export ### Data: interactive import Use **`file.choose()`** to select a file manually: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df = read.csv(file.choose()) ``` ::: The **RStudio menu** also offers **File > Import Dataset**, with options for text, Excel and SPSS files. Keep the resulting import code in your script. A saved relative path makes rerunning the analysis possible without selecting the file again. ## Import/export ### Data You have processed data with R, now... how to **export** it? When collaborating with someone also using R, you may choose to exchange data directly by exporting the object or the entire workspace as a `.RData` file, using the `save()` or `save.image()` functions, respectively. However, if you need to export a dataframe in a more universally readable tabular format, such as `.csv`, you may use **`write.csv()`**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # specify the dataframe to export (here named "df") # along with the desired file name, and other arguments write.csv(df, file="myExportedData.csv") # if you don't want row numbering / row names write.csv(df, file="myExportedData.csv", row.names=F) ``` ::: ## Import/export ### Figures R has a collection of functions for exporting figures in different formats: `pdf()`, `png()`, `jpeg()`, `bmp()`, `tiff()`, `svg()`. Here is an example using `png()`. We use quick base R plots to check data; figure design is covered in the **ggplot2 course**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # set up a graphic output file named "MyFigure.png" with some settings png("MyFigure.png", height=1500, width=2000, units="px", res=300) # code for creating a simple boxplot boxplot(iris$Sepal.Width) # close the graphic output file and actually export the plot dev.off() ``` :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
